summary:
Problem: Space mission design requires balancing competing engineering demands—including mass, power, budget, propulsion thrust, and scientific payload selection—yet students rarely get to experiment with an entire mission from concept to operation. Existing learning tools typically isolate single concepts rather than showing how engineering trade-offs interact as a complete system.

Solution: OrbitOps is an interactive Space Mission Design Game that lets players plan, assemble, and simulate end-to-end NASA-inspired missions across our Solar System and beyond. Players select a planetary target, configure modular spacecraft components (core hull, thermal shields, aerodynamic surfaces, propulsion, and power systems), and equip real scientific instruments while staying within strict mass, thrust, power, and budget constraints.

Grounded directly in real metrics from the NASA Planetary Fact Sheet, NASA Exoplanet Archive, Planetary Data System (PDS), and Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS), the simulation evaluates every build against authentic environmental hazards—such as Venus’s 92-bar pressure and sulfuric acid clouds or Kepler’s 0.003-arcsecond pointing stability. When a mission fails, a diagnostic screen explains the exact physics behind the failure so players can adapt, rebuild, and unlock real 2026 NASA discoveries.
details:
Orbit Ops
Orbit Ops is a single-player spacecraft-design game that introduces players to the trade-offs involved in planning a planetary science mission. Players choose Mars, Venus, or Neptune, review the mission objectives and environmental hazards, then assemble a spacecraft by selecting its head, body, wings, engine, and scientific instrument.

Each component affects spacecraft cost, mass, and engineering stats such as heat resistance, cold resistance, durability, and control. Players must keep their build within its budget and mass limit, then test their timing in a launch challenge. The outcome depends on both spacecraft readiness and the player’s timing; a successful mission can then use its instrument to investigate the science target. A report explains the result and tracks mission records and best scores.

Benefits and intended impact: Orbit Ops makes mission planning approachable and interactive. It encourages players to consider how engineering decisions affect mission success, introduces planetary conditions and scientific instruments, and turns failure into a chance to learn. The intended impact is to spark curiosity about space exploration, science, and systems engineering—especially for players who may find technical topics easier to engage with through a game.

Tools and technology: The game was developed with React, TypeScript, and Vite, using Zustand for in-memory game state, Material UI for interface components, Framer Motion for animation, and Vitest for tests. It runs in a web browser and is designed for static deployment. It does not use a database or save progress in local storage, and no special hardware is required.

What makes it creative: Orbit Ops combines a visual spacecraft builder, real-time launch-timing challenge, animated mission sequences, and science-result screens into one connected experience. Its layered spacecraft preview changes as parts are selected, while mission-specific scenes and outcomes help make each destination feel distinct.

Factors considered: We considered each destination’s conditions and hazards, the trade-offs among component mass, cost, and stats, clear explanations of mission odds and failure outcomes, and accessible presentation. The game also respects reduced-motion preferences and keeps all state local to the current session.
